name: Zinfandel

lines.s10: Zinfandel is the red California made its own: brambly blackberry jam and black pepper with a raisin edge, and Italy calls it Primitivo.
lines.s20: Zinfandel came from Croatia, but it is at home in the old vineyards of California and, as Primitivo, in the heel of Italy. It tastes of blackberry jam, raspberry and black pepper, with moderate tannin and a warm finish.
lines.s45: Zinfandel reached California in the Gold Rush, and old, gnarled vines still grow in Lodi, Sonoma and the Sierra Foothills. It tastes of blackberry jam, raspberry and black pepper. Its bunches ripen unevenly, which often leaves a raisin edge. The colour is only medium and the tannin moderate, but the alcohol is high. American oak often adds vanilla and a hint of dill. In Puglia, where it is called Primitivo, it tends to be more savoury, with leather and tobacco. It belongs with barbecue: smoky ribs, a spiced sausage or a burger. DNA finally traced it home to Croatia, where old records call it Tribidrag.
lines.sale: Smoke and a sweet, sticky glaze want a red with ripe fruit and a little pepper, and Zinfandel brings both. With the ribs or a spiced sausage, I would serve it a touch cool so the warmth stays in check.

glass.lead: Brambly blackberry jam and raspberry with black pepper and a raisin edge, on a full, warm body of only medium colour.

ladder.where: Gioia del Colle, on the limestone plateau of the Murge
Manduria, Lodi, Amador, Paso Robles and Dry Creek Valley

glass.structure: Dry. Acidity medium to medium plus, tannin medium to medium plus, alcohol high, body full.

old.where: Puglia, as Primitivo: Manduria on the Ionian coast and Gioia del Colle
old.glass: Tends to be more savoury and rustic: black plum, black cherry and dried fig with leather and tobacco leaf, and alcohol often nearly as high as California's.
old.cellar: Labelled Primitivo with its place. Old vines are often bush vines, and Manduria also makes a sweet red, Dolce Naturale, from late picked or dried grapes.

new.where: California: Lodi, Sonoma's Dry Creek Valley, Amador and Paso Robles
new.glass: Typically riper and jammier: blackberry jam, raspberry and a raisin edge with black pepper, then vanilla and dill from American oak, and high alcohol.
new.cellar: Bottled under the grape's own name, often from old head trained vines, some in field blends with Petite Sirah and Carignane; usually aged in oak, often American.

contrast.why: Both homes are hot, so alcohol runs high on either side. California tends to pick riper, for jammier fruit, and to age in American oak, for vanilla. Puglia's label names the place, California's the grape.
contrast.blur: Some Puglian cellars pick very ripe and use new oak, for a plush Primitivo hard to tell from California, while some California cellars now pick earlier for fresher wines.
contrast.call: Leather, tobacco leaf and a savoury, dry finish lean Puglia; blackberry jam with vanilla and dill up front leans California.

service.temp: 61 to 64 degrees Fahrenheit, 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; the cooler end keeps the alcohol in check.
service.glass: A Bordeaux glass, filled no more than a third.
service.decant: Usually unnecessary for a fruity young wine; taste a sample first, and decant an old bottle off its sediment.
service.age: Most show well at three to eight years; a few old vine wines keep longer.

with.why: ripe fruit stands up to smoke and a sweet glaze
black pepper in the wine meets the spice
char and fat suit the brambly fruit
slow cooked meat for a ripe red

labels.means: The Italian name of the same grape, at home in Puglia; it is named for ripening early.
Dry Primitivo from the Ionian coast of Taranto and Brindisi; the sweet one is the Dolce Naturale.
A term with no legal definition in the United States, often taken to mean vines of fifty years or more.
An off dry pink made from the same grape, its juice taken off the skins early; not a separate grape.

guest.q: Is Zinfandel the sweet pink wine?
guest.a: That is White Zinfandel, an off dry pink made from the same grape. Red Zinfandel is dry and full bodied, with blackberry jam, black pepper and a warm finish.

guest.q: Is Primitivo the same as Zinfandel?
guest.a: Yes, one grape: DNA work at the University of California, Davis showed it, and traced both to Croatia. Primitivo tends to be the more savoury.
Its bunches ripen unevenly, so growers wait for the last berries while others turn to raisins, and all that sugar becomes alcohol.
By long history it is California's, but it came from Croatia, by way of a Vienna nursery and Long Island in the 1820s, and reached California in the Gold Rush.

compare.tell: Grenache is paler, with kirsch, strawberry and dried thyme; Zinfandel is darker and jammier, with blackberry, a raisin edge and black pepper.
Syrah is darker and more savoury, with smoked meat, black olive and firmer tannin; Zinfandel is jammier, with a raisin edge and only medium colour.
Corvina, as Amarone, shares the raisin edge but adds sour cherry and bitter almond; Zinfandel is brambly, with blackberry jam and black pepper.

cards.front: Zinfandel: its Italian and Croatian names, and where it began?
cards.back: Primitivo in Puglia; Tribidrag, also called Crljenak Kaštelanski, in Croatia, where it began. DNA work at the University of California, Davis showed all three are one grape.

cards.front: Zinfandel blind: Primitivo from Puglia or California, what tips it?
cards.back: Leather, tobacco leaf and a savoury, dry finish lean Puglia. Blackberry jam with vanilla and dill from American oak up front leans California. Alcohol runs high in both.

cards.front: Why does Zinfandel so often show a raisin edge and high alcohol?
cards.back: Its bunches ripen unevenly: some berries shrivel to raisins while others are still catching up, and the sugar of the ripest becomes alcohol.

questions.q: Two glasses of the same grape are poured blind. One shows leather, tobacco leaf and dried fig with a savoury finish; the other blackberry jam, vanilla and dill. Which pair of origins fits, in that order?
opts: Primitivo di Manduria, then Lodi Zinfandel
Lodi Zinfandel, then Primitivo di Manduria
Dry Creek Valley, then Paso Robles
questions.exp: Leather, tobacco and a savoury finish tend to mark Puglian Primitivo; blackberry jam with vanilla and dill from American oak tends to mark California. Two California sites, or two Puglian ones, would not split this way.

questions.q: A guest's friend in Bari recommended Primitivo, and your list holds none. Which bottle on the list is the same grape?
opts: A Zinfandel from Dry Creek Valley
A Petite Sirah from Napa Valley
questions.exp: Primitivo and Zinfandel are one grape, shown by DNA. Petite Sirah often grows beside Zinfandel in old California vineyards but is a separate grape, a child of Syrah, and Negroamaro is Puglia's other red.

questions.q: A blind red of only medium colour shows blackberry jam, raspberry and a raisin edge, with black pepper and a warm, high alcohol finish. Which grape fits?
questions.exp: Jammy, brambly fruit with a raisin edge and high alcohol at only medium colour is Zinfandel. Grenache would be paler, with kirsch and dried thyme; Syrah and Petite Sirah would be darker.

report: Mode contrast, as the plan fixes it: Primitivo from Puglia against California. TASTE.world reads new, which the side by side does not contradict, since the grape's Old World style is Italian; a reviewer may wish TASTE.world to read both, as the plan's own rule for a side by side suggests.
Say opens on the Court's own ZIN-fan-del and adds pree-mee-TEE-voh, the Italian name a guest meets on a label.

The Codex's dials disagree with its own prose on tannin: TASTE gives Zinfandel tan 1, medium minus, while GRAPES reads tannin medium to medium plus, INTRO_GRAPES gives 2 and the Court's grid read gives medium and medium plus. The entry follows GRAPES and the grid.

The ladder has two rungs and no cool one. The Court's grid reads Napa and Sonoma as warm for Zinfandel, so Dry Creek Valley stands on the warm rung with Manduria, Lodi, Amador and Paso Robles. The moderate rung is Gioia del Colle alone, on the Codex's own reviewed Puglia article: the Murge at around 300 to 500 metres gives the freshest Primitivo in Puglia. Mendocino and the Santa Cruz Mountains are often taught as cooler Zinfandel sites but were not confirmed in this session and are left out; raspberry, red cherry and black pepper on that rung rest on fresher, not on a tasting note read.

The Primitivo style, more savoury and rustic with leather, tobacco leaf and dried fig, and California riper and jammier with sweeter oak, stands on a retailer's guide and three trade pages read through search, not on a wine body; they disagree on which side has the higher acidity, so no acidity is claimed, and no page settled whether Primitivo is typically less oaked, so the entry does not say so. The blur's plush, new oak Primitivo stands on a Manduria tasting note of fig, blackberry jam and vanilla read through search; a checker may wish a firmer source.

Primitivo di Manduria at the Ionian coast of Taranto and Brindisi, the sweet Dolce Naturale from late picked or dried grapes, bush vines among the old Puglian vineyards and Primitivo named for ripening early are the Codex's own reviewed facts in the Puglia article. Tribidrag as the oldest name and Crljenak Kastelanski are the Codex's own too.

The history: cuttings from the imperial nursery collection in Vienna reached a Long Island nursery in the 1820s, and the vine reached California in the Gold Rush. Pages read through search agree on the decade and differ on the year, from 1820 to 1829; one account dates the shipment west from Boston to 1852. No year and nobody is named.

The DNA work: pages read through search agree that researchers at the University of California, Davis showed Zinfandel and Primitivo to be one grape and matched it to Crljenak Kastelanski on the Dalmatian coast of Croatia; they differ on the years, so none is given. The earliest record of the name Tribidrag is given as the fifteenth century on one page and 1518 on another, so no date is given.

Old Vine with no legal definition in the United States stands on Decanter, on VinePair and on the Zinfandel body's own pages; the fifty year line is a trade convention, which the label hedges as often taken to mean.
White Zinfandel is given only as the Codex's own trap states it, an off dry pink of the same grape; its origin in the 1970s was not confirmed and is left out.
Coconut beside vanilla and dill from American oak is common tasting teaching; the Codex's own GRAPES record names vanilla and dill.

Compare names Corvina, as Amarone, outside the plan's candidates, because the Codex's own GRAPES and GRAPES_PLUS records name Amarone's raisined fruit as the confusion. Petite Sirah, a plan candidate, appears in the cellar line and a question instead.
No Creole dish is given: high alcohol can sharpen chilli heat, as the Codex's own pairing notes warn, and ribs, sausage and a burger suit the grape better than any of the seven.
The sources were read through search results; this session could not open zinfandel.org, which is outside the session's allowed network.

checked.verdict: Sound after two fixes in one round. Primitivo and Tribidrag as one vine, the Vienna nursery and Long Island in the 1820s, the Gold Rush, Manduria and Gioia del Colle, the Dolce Naturale and Old Vine with no legal meaning were confirmed against the Codex's California and Puglia records; the spoken line called Tribidrag the oldest name where the records date its first mention differently, and the blur admitted the Old World's exception but not the New World's.
changed: lines.s45: Oldest reads as a superlative to the lint, and the records date the first mention of Tribidrag differently (the fifteenth century on one page, 1518 on another); old records call it states the fact without ranking it.

worlds.contrast.blur: The blur admitted only the Old World's exception. Since the big vintages of the late 1990s some California cellars pick two to three weeks earlier, with less new oak, for fresher wines; that is the New World's.
open: The Codex's Puglia record reads Primitivo inky where the reviewed profile reads Zinfandel medium to deep ruby, rarely opaque; the entry says nothing of Primitivo's colour.
